bull.argument: The filing shows a business with strong and accelerating momentum. Consolidated net sales grew 12% to $716.9 billion in 2025, and AWS sales grew 20% to $128.7 billion, with the segment's operating income rising to $45.6 billion. Total operating income rose from $68.6 billion to $80.0 billion, and operating cash flow climbed to $139.5 billion from $115.9 billion. Management is deliberately investing for the future: cash capital expenditures reached $128.3 billion, with the majority supporting AWS growth, and management expects these to increase in 2026. The company also guided first quarter 2026 net sales growth of 11% to 15%. Risks are real; the filing discusses intense competition, regulatory investigations, and the FTC settlement of $2.5 billion. But the company has a diversified base across North America, International, and AWS, and its cash generation funds that investment without relying on distressed financing. The filing also notes that the 2025 Tax Act significantly decreased cash taxes, supporting free cash flow.

claims.claim: AWS sales growth accelerated to 20% in 2025 with operating income rising to $45.6 billion.
claims.quote: AWS sales increased 20% in 2025, compared to the prior year. The sales growth primarily reflects increased customer usage

claims.claim: Operating cash flow rose to $139.5 billion in 2025 from $115.9 billion in 2024, funding heavy investment.
claims.quote: Cash provided by (used in) operating activities was $115.9 billion and $139.5 billion in 2024 and 2025.

claims.claim: Management expects capital investment in infrastructure to rise, reflecting confidence in long-term demand.
claims.quote: which primarily reflect investments in technology infrastructure (the majority of which is to support AWS business growth)

bear.argument: The filing's own numbers show the cash engine shrinking relative to spending. Free cash flow fell from $38.2 billion in 2024 to $11.2 billion in 2025, because cash capital expenditures jumped to $128.3 billion, and management says these will increase in 2026. Operating income grew, but it was carried by AWS, while the filing states that 'a significant portion of our expenses and investments is fixed' and that sales could fall short of plans. Technology and infrastructure costs rose 23% and other operating expense rose 508%, including a $2.5 billion FTC settlement and $2.7 billion of severance. Financing is also moving: long-term debt rose from $52.6 billion to $65.6 billion and the company raised $25.0 billion in debt in 2025. Other income of $15.2 billion came mainly from valuation adjustments on an Anthropic investment, not operations. The filing also warns that AI investments 'may not meet our expectations' and could be 'written down or written off.' Investors are paying for a spending cycle whose payoff is uncertain.

claims.claim: Free cash flow collapsed as capital spending surged, undermining the cash-generation story.
Management warns AI and new-technology investments may fail to pay back and could be written off.
claims.quote: Failure to realize the benefits of amounts we invest in new technologies, products, or services could result in the value of those investments being written down or written off.

claims.claim: Debt is rising to help fund the spending, and the company will keep raising capital as needed.
claims.quote: Cash inflows from financing activities resulted from proceeds from short-term debt, and other and long-term-debt of $5.1 billion and $25.0 billion in 2024 and 2025.

bull.argument: The opponent is right that free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion from $38.2 billion, and I should not hide that. But the decline is the product of deliberate investment in a business that is already earning returns. AWS sales grew 20% to $128.7 billion and its operating income rose to $45.6 billion, so the segment funding the infrastructure build is itself profitable. Operating cash flow still climbed to $139.5 billion, meaning the company generated more cash from operations and chose to reinvest it. The debt increase is modest relative to that cash flow, and the company reports no borrowings under its revolving facilities or commercial paper programs at year-end. The $15.2 billion other income is non-operating, and I concede it should be discounted; the $80.0 billion operating income figure is the better measure of the core business. The filing's risk warnings on AI write-downs are real, but they describe possibilities, not current losses. The bull case rests on operating results that are growing, not on the investment outcome being guaranteed.

claims.claim: AWS operating income rose to $45.6 billion alongside 20% sales growth, showing the segment funding the build-out is profitable.
claims.quote: AWS sales increased 20% in 2025, compared to the prior year. The sales growth primarily reflects increased customer usage

claims.claim: Operating cash flow rose to $139.5 billion, so the company generated more cash from operations even as it reinvested.
claims.quote: Cash provided by (used in) operating activities was $115.9 billion and $139.5 billion in 2024 and 2025.

claims.claim: The company reported no borrowings outstanding under its revolving credit facilities or commercial paper programs at year-end 2025.
claims.quote: We had no borrowings outstanding under the two unsecured revolving credit facilities or the commercial paper programs as of December 31, 2025.

bear.argument: The bull case depends on the spending paying off, and the filing does not show that yet. The opponent concedes free cash flow fell from $38.2 billion to $11.2 billion, a drop of about 71%. Operating cash flow rising to $139.5 billion does not help shareholders if it is fully absorbed by $128.3 billion of capital expenditures. Calling this a choice to reinvest does not change that the owner's residual cash shrank. AWS profitability is real, but the filing says AWS operating income rose on 'spending on technology infrastructure' that is growing, and it says technology and infrastructure costs jumped 23%. The filing also says cash capex will 'increase in 2026' and guides to a $1 billion rise in Amazon Leo costs, so the spending cycle is not ending. The debt point is less comforting than presented: long-term debt rose from $52.6 billion to $65.6 billion, and the company raised $25.0 billion in 2025. Management's own warning that new-technology investments 'may not meet our expectations' remains the central risk, and it is not a remote possibility given these magnitudes.

claims.claim: Free cash flow fell by roughly 71% as capital spending absorbed operating cash.
Management expects capital spending to rise further in 2026, extending the period of weak free cash flow.
claims.quote: both of which we expect to increase in 2026

claims.claim: Management warns that investments in new technologies may not pay back and could be written off.
claims.quote: profitability or other intended benefits, if any, in our newer activities (including development and adoption of automation, artificial intelligence, and machine learning technologies), may not meet our expectations

judge.reasoning: Both sides cite verified quotes, but the bear's evidence is more directly on point, centering on the 71% free cash flow collapse and explicit management warnings about write-offs that the bull only partially rebuts. The bull concedes the free cash flow decline and the non-operating nature of other income, and its no-borrowings point is a useful counter, but it leans on operating cash flow and segment profit without fully answering why reinvestment absorbing all operating cash should reassure owners. The bear's rebuttal on rising debt and 2026 capex guidance is more persuasive on the logic of cash to shareholders.
